problem: Evolve molecular property prediction models for ADMET (Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism, Excretion, Toxicity) endpoints critical to drug discovery. Focus on hERG cardiac toxicity, a major cause of drug candidate attrition.

population.description: Added 8 molecular descriptors (MW, LogP, TPSA, H-bond donors/acceptors, rotatable bonds, aromatic/aliphatic rings) to complement Morgan fingerprints, increasing feature dimensionality from 2048 to 2056
population.hypothesis: Molecular descriptors provide interpretable physicochemical properties that complement the structural patterns captured by fingerprints. This richer feature representation should improve model performance on hERG prediction by capturing drug-like properties and ADMET-relevant molecular characteristics that pure fingerprints might miss.
population.notes: Strong performance with ROC-AUC 0.859, good cross-validation stability (CV mean: 0.867, std: 0.028)
population.adversary_analysis: The candidate solution shows a legitimate and well-reasoned improvement over the parent. The key changes are: (1) Addition of 8 molecular descriptors (MW, LogP, TPSA, H-bond donors/acceptors, rotatable bonds, aromatic/aliphatic rings) that are standard in ADMET prediction, (2) Enhanced feature engineering that concatenates fingerprints with descriptors, expanding feature space from 2048 to 2056 dimensions, (3) Proper error handling for invalid molecules with zero-padding. The claimed hypothesis aligns perfectly with the implementation - using molecular descriptors to complement structural fingerprints is a established cheminformatics practice. The 85.9% fitness improvement from 0% to 85.9% is substantial but explainable: the parent had 0% fitness (likely a baseline/failed run), and the addition of physicochemical descriptors provides meaningful signal for hERG prediction. The descriptors chosen (MW, LogP, TPSA, etc.) are directly relevant to drug cardiotoxicity prediction. No red flags detected: no hardcoded values, no lookup tables, no timing exploits, legitimate algorithmic enhancement. The improvement is incremental and follows established domain knowledge. Cross-validation stability (mean: 0.867, std: 0.028) suggests good generalization. Minor trust reduction only due to the large absolute improvement magnitude, but this is justified given the parent's zero baseline performance.
